hints: Break structure P into parts, two $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4$ rings plus one $\text{CH}_2$ bridge plus two $\text{NCO}$ groups, and count C, H, N and O carefully.
walkthrough:
Count the skeleton piece by piece**
Sit with structure P and do not try to count all at once. Each para-disubstituted benzene is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4$, so two of them give $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_8$. The bridge between them is $\text{CH}_2$, taking you to $\text{C}_{13}\text{H}_{10}$. Then add the two isocyanate ends, $2 \times \text{NCO}$, which add $\text{C}_2\text{N}_2\text{O}_2$. Put it together to get $\text{C}_{15}\text{H}_{10}\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{2}$.

hints: Compare the general equation to this example and identify what $\text{R}^1$ and $\text{R}^2$ are, $\text{R}^1$ is the central part of P and $\text{R}^2$ is from $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.
Recall that no small molecule is lost here, the $\text{N=C=O}$ plus $\text{HO-}$ rearranges directly to $\text{-NH-CO-O-}$, so join the fragments in that order.
walkthrough:
See how the urethane link forms**
The general equation shows $\text{O=C=N-}$ + $\text{HO-}$ becoming $\text{-C(=O)-NH-O-}$. Think of the H from the alcohol moving onto the N, and the O from the alcohol bonding to the C=O carbon. That $\text{-NH-CO-O-}$ group is the fingerprint of every polyurethane.

Plug in the two R groups**
Here $\text{R}^1$ is everything left in P after removing the two $\text{NCO}$ carbons, that is $\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CH}_2\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-}$. And $\text{R}^2$ is everything left in $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ after removing the two OH oxygens, that is $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-}$. Fit them into the general bracket: $\text{-[C(=O)-NH-R}^1\text{-NH-C(=O)-O-R}^2\text{-O]-}$.

Write the full repeat unit**
Substituting gives $\text{-[C(=O)-NH-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CH}_2\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NH-C(=O)-O-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-O]-}$. Draw the two benzene rings para substituted, keep both $\text{NH}$ groups with H shown, keep both $\text{C=O}$ groups, and close the section with continuation bonds through the outer O atoms.
Final answer: Repeat unit: $\text{-[CO-NH-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CH}_2\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NH-CO-O-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-O]-}$ containing two urethane linkages $\text{-NH-CO-O-}$.

hints: Look for polar $\text{N-H}$ donors and $\text{C=O}$ acceptors in the urethane link and recall which strong intermolecular force they can set up between chains.
Look at the large non-polar hydrocarbon part, the two benzene rings and $\text{CH}_2$ groups, and recall which force acts between all such electron clouds.
walkthrough:
Spot the hydrogen bonding sites**
Each urethane link has $\text{-N-H}$ where N is bonded directly to H, plus a highly polar $\text{C=O}$. Between neighbouring chains the $\text{N-H}$ hydrogen, with its partial positive charge, is strongly attracted to a lone pair on a $\text{C=O}$ oxygen on the next chain. That is classic $\text{N-H} \cdots \text{O=C}$ hydrogen bonding, and with many such links along long chains it holds the fibres very firmly together.

Add the second attraction from the rings**
The polymer also contains large flat $\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CH}_2\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-}$ sections. These non-polar aromatic regions cannot hydrogen bond, but their large electron clouds give extensive temporary dipoles. That creates London dispersion (induced dipole-dipole, van der Waals) forces between chains, reinforced by close packing of the rings. Together the two forces explain the high strength.

Final answer: Hydrogen bonding involving $\text{NH}$ groups (with $\text{C=O}$ as acceptor) between chains.
London dispersion / induced dipole-dipole forces (van der Waals) involving the aromatic $\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}_2\text{-}$ groups.

hints: For the two condensation types, think of the most famous A Level examples, a nylon or Kevlar for amide links and Terylene (PET) for ester links.
For conduction, think which polymer has a long chain of alternating double bonds with delocalised p electrons that can move.
For non-solvent based adhesive, think of glues that harden by chemical reaction or polymerisation in place, not by evaporation, such as epoxy or superglue.
walkthrough:
Recall the classic condensation polymers**
A synthetic polyamide is built from amide $\text{-CO-NH-}$ links made in the lab. Nylon-6,6, nylon-6 and the aromatic polyamide Kevlar are all perfect answers. A synthetic polyester is built from ester $\text{-CO-O-}$ links. Terylene, also called PET or Dacron, is the standard example you meet in the syllabus.

Pick the delocalised chain for conduction**
Most polymers are insulators because all electrons are localised in sigma bonds. A conducting polymer needs conjugation along the backbone so electrons can move. Polyacetylene, also named polyethyne, $\text{-(CH=CH)}_n\text{-}$, is the textbook case.

Pick a reactive adhesive**
A non-solvent based adhesive does not set by losing solvent, it sets by crosslinking or rapid polymerisation. Epoxy resins (two-part resin plus hardener) and superglue (cyanoacrylate that polymerises with moisture) are the accepted examples. Any three correct pairings earn the three marks.

Final answer: synthetic polyamide: nylon-6,6 / nylon-6 / Kevlar
synthetic polyester: Terylene / PET / poly(ethylene terephthalate)
conducting polymer: polyacetylene / polyethyne
non-solvent based adhesive: epoxy resin / superglue
